DUBAI/LONDON/WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing ⁠through the ⁠Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high ⁠and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.

Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US and ​Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.

Its threats and attacks ‌have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil ‌prices, though some oil has continued to transit.

The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 ⁠days ago, adding that this ⁠had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.

The strategy included a change in the type as well as the ​pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.

"The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices," one of the two officials said.

The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials said.

IRAN USING SPOTTERS

A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Iran had changed tactics in one significant ​way: after the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels, the official ⁠said.

Last ⁠week, in a previously unreported incident, the US ⁠military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a ​dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US ​official said.

Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran had been ⁠unable to prevent a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official said, particularly after US strikes devastated its navy.

The war — and its $3 billion monthly price tag — has become a key issue on the US campaign trail for November's midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress.

US President Donald Trump has been weighing next steps against Iran, but has said he will not attack again before the vote.

The US has meanwhile been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports and extending sanctions as it tries to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict.

The standoff over Hormuz has left global energy markets exposed to further disruption, with the threat of attacks and high shipping and ⁠insurance costs complicating efforts to restore normal traffic.

In recent days, attacks on commercial ships still sailing through the strait have surged to their highest level since ⁠the war began, according to independent data.

There have been at least five incidents in the past 48 hours involving tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area, including drone strikes, according to data analysis from maritime security sources and incidents reported to British navy-affiliated agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).

It turns out that F1 is mathematically the most dramatic sport.

I'm not an F1 fan myself, but the data is unequivocal.

The proof: take a time series of prediction market data and measure the volatility minute-by-minute in the odds for each sport. This measures the density of actual drama in the sport during a game. 

Even if there's action and points going back and forth on screen, it's meaningless if the winner is basically decided. It's only real drama when the odds are moving in realtime while you're watching.

By this metric: F1 > E-sports (CS2) > Soccer > Basketball > Tennis > American football > Baseball >>> Golf

That's right, golf is mathematically the worst sport.

(I knew it.)

a16z crypto's Eddy Lazzarin on why AI makes the world more secure: bugs are finite, and the cost of finding them keeps collapsing.

"Making comparisons between models from a year ago versus today... Some people were coming up with estimates like it's... 99% cheaper for intellectual capability per dollar."

"Pair that with a frame we've talked about before, which is that the number of bugs in software is finite. Then we're asymptotically approaching zero bugs. Maybe we actually just hit zero at some point."

"If that's the case, we are net improving the security status of the world instead of eroding it."

"This is not a battle of wits where you have a system, I have a system, your system is smarter than mine, therefore I am vulnerable to you... That relies on there being vulnerabilities, and vulnerabilities can be removed."

"The primary resource we dedicate to mitigating it is a thing that's getting radically cheaper every couple months. That's AI."

Dan Boneh: "Companies actually are already doing this. They're spending a lot of money on scanning their code base with the latest models... Every time there's a software update... Every time a new model comes out, they scan the software again."

@eddylazzarin @danboneh

a16z crypto's Eddy Lazzarin and Stanford's Dan Boneh on how AI's math leap could turn a decade of trust-building in cryptography into one month:

Eddy: "We specifically rely in some sense on time... We put these schemes out and we wait. And we wait because what we believe is happening is that experts, like cryptographers and mathematicians, are testing and trying to break these things."

"Because of the pace of progress on AI's mathematical abilities, there is a conspicuous absence of time... A whole new well of cognitive ability to scrutinize has appeared."

Dan: "In the past, when someone would make an assumption and build a system based on it, we'd have to wait like 10 years before that system could be deployed."

"Now we can just let a model run for a month, try to break it, and if the model can't break it, boy, do we have a lot of confidence that the assumption is valid."

Eddy: "The labs can say, 'We took our tip-top, totally unrestricted, most cyber-capable model, and we told it to go absolutely insane, and we spent $20 million, $50 million trying to break this scheme.'"

"We actually have the prospect to have more confidence in our security than ever before."

@eddylazzarin @danboneh

$BTC and alts are pulling back again, and people are already panicking.

Most people won't make it to the next cycle with their gains intact.

10 lessons to make sure you're not one of them:

1. Stop trying to follow every sector.

Pick 2-3 and get to know them better than most people do. You'll find more opportunities that way than by chasing whatever CT is yelling about today.

"I fear not the man who has practiced 10,000 kicks once, but I fear the man who has practiced one kick 10,000 times." - Bruce Lee

2. Pay attention to macro, even if you hate it.

Crypto keeps getting more tied to how much cheap money is floating around (interest rates, ETF flows, that kinda stuff). Nobody's asking you to predict the Fed. 

You just need a rough sense of what's actually moving the market.

3. The next big narrative won't save your old bags.

Money is jumping between AI, RWAs, perps, and memecoins faster than ever. Your token pumped in 2021? Cool, that doesn't mean anyone wants it in 2026.

4. A good product doesn't always mean a good token.

A protocol can make millions in revenue while token holders never see a dollar of it. 

So before you buy, ask the boring question… where does the money actually go?

5. Don't buy a token just because it announced buybacks.

If a project buys back $10M while unlocking $50M worth of tokens, you're still getting diluted. Check the unlock schedule before you get excited.

6. Be careful when everyone starts calling a token undervalued.

5x annual revenue looks cheap right up until that revenue drops 70% next month. Cheap on paper doesn't mean much if the business can't keep making money.

7. Know how long you're holding before you buy.

Some tokens are worth holding for years and some for a few weeks, and you should know which one you're buying going in. 

Don't turn a short-term trade into a long-term investment just because the price went down. Honestly, that's how most bags get made.

8. Decide your exit before you enter.

Know your profit target and what would make you sell if the trade goes against you. Otherwise you'll keep moving the goalposts every time the price moves.

"The investor's chief problem, and even his worst enemy, is likely to be himself." - Benjamin Graham

9. Rotating profits into riskier tokens is just moving to another table at the casino.

Actually lock some of those gains into BTC, stablecoins, or fiat.

10. Protect your capital like your life depends on it.

You don't need to catch every 100x or every new narrative. Missing a pump stings for a week or so, but blowing up your portfolio is the kind of mistake that sets you back years.

"The first rule of compounding is to never interrupt it unnecessarily." - Charlie Munger

I still think the opportunity in DeFi is huge. We've got real businesses, institutional money coming in, stablecoins getting used for everyday payments, and financial assets moving onchain, and the basics still apply to all of it.

Make the money when it's there, and when things get ugly, focus on protecting it so you're still around for the next run.

What's one lesson crypto taught you the hard way?

everyone wants to be right as a bear. calling the top is more validating than calling the rally, because you get to play the wiser, higher-than-thou observer who watched humanity get greedy and slaughtered once again while you refused to give in to the mania.

so you'll find plenty of people hunting for the pin that pops the bubble. and yes, eventually there is a pin and the bubble does pop. but somehow it's fine to call 99 bear markets that never came as long as you nail one, as if it were a matter of life and death. in this version of the story the boy who cried wolf survives, and everyone who ignored him gets eaten. that's hardly true unless you're levered to the tits.

i'd rather be invested in the bubble, ideally a big one with plenty of room left to grow. 

i've stopped trying to feel clever about how i make money. i take the long view that things will be fine and that humanity has a way of progressing, and i let the index and a long time horizon cover for my lapses in judgment and analysis. my models and forecasts are as good as anyone's. my edge is being willing to hold for a really long time

My bet: AI feeds will be the biggest form factor of 2027. People spend all day scrolling Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, Twitter. They know how a feed works. They don’t want to learn how to prompt AI, they want it to do stuff for them.

Personal agents are starting to send proactive messages. Cool, but do I want more notifications? No. I want more than a push message. 

If AI knows me and is actually smart, give me a feed of things I care about and things I need to do. Reply to this email? Book this? Here’s something you should know.

Swipe right, left, yes, no. Get stuff done. Also, feeds unlock ads. Ads make AI free. 

Why hasn’t it happened yet?

1/ Context. You need an agent that knows you through thousands of chats + your email, calendar, etc. Almost nobody has all that connected yet so the market is too small. But personal agents are getting us there.

2/ COGS. You can’t spend $$$ generating a feed you need to refresh all day. But small models are getting smart enough to make this work.

We already have the scrolling habit. Now we’re getting the AI to make it useful imo.
